title: The Growth Ladder
blurb: Before you can name a complexity, you need the pecking order. Put these from fastest-growing-slowest (best) at the top to fastest-growing (worst) at the bottom. Hover the ⓘ for what each one means.

docs.label: Big-O Cheat Sheet — the growth chart

glossary.O(1): Constant — the work doesn't grow with the input at all. An array index, a dictionary lookup, a fixed formula.
glossary.O(log n): Logarithmic — each step throws away a fraction (usually half) of what's left. Binary search. Barely grows.
glossary.O(n): Linear — the work grows in step with the input. One pass over the list.
glossary.O(n log n): Linearithmic — a linear amount of work done log n times. Efficient sorting (merge/quick sort).
glossary.O(n²): Quadratic — work grows with the square of the input. Nested loops over the same data.
glossary.O(2ⁿ): Exponential — the work doubles with each element added. Brute-forcing every subset; naive recursion. Avoid.

levels.title: L1 · The core four
levels.prompt: Slowest-growing (most efficient) at the top, fastest-growing at the bottom.
levels.hint: Ask what each does per element as n grows: fixed work, halving, one-per-element, or one-per-pair.
levels.explain: Most efficient to least: O(1) does fixed work, O(log n) barely grows (it halves each step), O(n) grows in step with the input, and O(n²) grows with its square. That’s the order their curves cross as n gets large.

failStates.title: log n grows slower than n
failStates.explain: O(log n) barely grows — doubling the input adds just one step. It's more efficient than O(n), so it sits above it.

failStates.title: Quadratic is worse than linear
failStates.explain: For large n, n² dwarfs n (a million items → a trillion operations). O(n²) is the least efficient here, so it goes at the bottom.

levels.title: L2 · The full ladder
levels.prompt: Add the linearithmic and exponential rungs. Best (top) to worst (bottom).
levels.hint: Rank by how fast the curve climbs. Two have a log factor; one explodes past every polynomial.
levels.explain: The full order, best to worst: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ). Each grows strictly faster than the one before, and O(2ⁿ) eventually dwarfs every polynomial.

failStates.title: n log n beats n²
failStates.explain: n log n is only a little worse than linear (the extra log n factor). n² is far worse — it belongs below n log n. This gap is exactly why an O(n log n) sort beats an O(n²) one.

failStates.title: Exponential is the worst
failStates.explain: 2ⁿ explodes — 30 items is already a billion operations. It grows faster than any polynomial, so O(2ⁿ) goes dead last.

failStates.title: Plain n is faster than n log n
failStates.explain: O(n) has no log factor, so it's more efficient than O(n log n) — linear sits above linearithmic.
